# Physiology, Breast Milk

**Authors:** Sarah Sabir, Ali F. Alhawaj

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Breast milk production begins in significant amounts between 2 and 4 days after birth, commonly described as the milk “coming in.” This process marks the transition from colostrum, the nutrient-rich early milk, to mature breast milk. Breast milk remains the optimal source of nutrition for infants, uniquely tailored to meet all nutritional, developmental, and immunological needs during early life. It supplies essential macronutrients, micronutrients, growth factors, hormones, and antibodies required for growth and protection against infection. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, followed by continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods up to 2 years of age or beyond [WHO, 2025 https://www.who.int/health-topics/breastfeeding#tab=tab_1; PAHO, 2025 https://www.paho.org/en/topics/breastfeeding-and-complementary-feeding]. Current global estimates show that approximately 48% of infants younger than 6 months are exclusively breastfed, approaching the World Health Assembly’s 2025 target of 50%. Recent studies have highlighted that breast milk composition is far more dynamic than previously thought, influenced by maternal health, diet, circadian rhythm, and environmental factors. For instance, the bioactive components and microbiome of breast milk fluctuate between day and night, modulating the infant’s metabolism and immune function. Genetic factors also play an emerging role in lactation variability; new research has identified gene expression patterns linked to milk production capacity. Beyond its nutritional function, breastfeeding has been associated with long-term health benefits for both the mother and child. Studies suggest that breastfeeding stimulates immune cell activity that may protect mothers against breast cancer, while infants benefit from enhanced immune regulation and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Furthermore, advancements in molecular biology have revealed that breast milk contains diverse cellular populations, including immune and stem cells, reflecting its complex physiological and regenerative nature. Collectively, these findings reinforce that breast milk is a living, adaptive biological fluid central to early human development. Ongoing global initiatives such as the WHO Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative and the Global Breastfeeding Collective continue to advocate for policies and programs that protect, promote, and support breastfeeding as a cornerstone of maternal and child health.
